newsitem.title: FRANCE: Good demand seen for French variable rate bond.
newsitem.headline: Good demand seen for French variable rate bond.

text.p: France's new variable rate government bond, the TEC 10, should continue to attract significant demand in 1997 even if the market environment becomes less favourable, analysts said.

Launched in April, the TEC 10 bond (taux de l'echeance constante 10 ans) which tracks an index of 10-year government bond yields, has been in such demand that after an initial syndicated issue, the Treasury offered it at every remaining monthly auction in 1996 with the exception of August.

Nearly 72 billion francs was issued in 1996 with a large majority ending up in domestic portfolios. Demand came mainly from French insurers, keen to protect themselves against an eventual rise in interest rates and fund managers playing on a steepening of the yield curve, analysts said.

Primary dealers said the Treasury was considering launching variable rate bonds based on indexes of 12- or 15-year government bond yields and had looked at a five-year floater in response to demand from primary dealers.
In 1997, "the Treasury should issue a fair amount of the TEC," said a primary dealer. He said primary dealers would be able to place 50 billion francs easily of the TEC 10 alone.
A swap trader at a large French bank said, "The outstanding is not that big compared with demand. We could reach 200 billion francs in this market and absorb it easily."

He said there were two factors explaining the success of the TEC 10, inspired by Constant Maturity Treasuries issued in the United States, which allowed it to spark a revival in the French variable rate market.
He said the choice of a clear reference with a transparent method of index fixing, unlike the case with the Treasury's previous variable rate bonds, or TMEs, was one reason for its success.
The second was that the TEC 10 met "a strong demand from insurers and besides that as a important trading vehicle for playing on a steepening of the yield curve," he said.
A mutual fund manager said, "Fund managers bought a lot this year to play yield curve steepening and to cover positions at the long-end (30-year) of the curve,"

"For 1997, the central hypothesis is a flattening of the curve, the margin for further declines in short-term interest rates appears limited. In this context, the product will be a little less attractive," he said. "But interest should persist because no-one expects a strong rebound in Europe."

The primary dealer said, "It's not ridiculous to have a certain percentage of a portfolio invested in variable rate instruments at a time when rates are historically low. To have five to 10 percent in variable rate paper is not a heresy, even if you do lose a (percentage) point of yield."

The swap trader said with the French bond market at its highs, which translates to the bond future trading between 125 and 130, the TEC will continue to stir interest. Only expectations of a strong economic rebound could provoke a mossive sell-off of paper which has good final demand.
"What's more, we could see a rush to the TEC 10 to begin with because if you think yields will go up, the variable rate will be in demand," he said.

However, a primary market trader said a small correction in the TEC 10, which most institutions consider to be some 60 centimes too expensive compared to its theoretical level, would aid interest in the bond.
Still, a bond trader at a French insurance group said, "It's expensive but that won't prevent people buying it because there's no other equivalent paper,"
A primary dealer said if there were a correction, "it will be more due to a change in the curve than from a lack of interest from investors".
